public_rationale: There is substantial evidence pointing toward the forecast. UK undergraduates reported major assessment changes, but those observations predate the post. Later US evidence shows widespread educator use and perceived time savings, without establishing the scale of changes in teaching or assessment. No reviewed event conclusively meets the early-resolution rule. The contextual five-year horizon has not elapsed.
limitations: This is not a finding that AI has had little impact on education.
The evidence covers particular countries and education levels and relies on self-reports.
The degree of change required by “large” remains interpretive.
If the panel's five-year framing does not bind this sentence, the forecast instead has an open horizon; it would still remain unresolved.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Marcus expects AI to have a large impact on education, though he adds words of caution.

statement.excerpt: And I turn out to be on the “large impact” side with respect to education:
statement.document_title: Where is AI headed? 8 perspectives at The New York Times

our_interpretation: The plain reading is that AI substantially changes teaching, learning, or assessment across a substantial part of education. Impact may be beneficial or harmful.
Words of caution do not identify an antecedent that must occur. This is not a conditional forecast.

The NYT panel's introduction, available in its syndicated Spanish translation, frames the exercise around the next five years. I apply that contextual horizon through February 2, 2031, although the individual education question supplies no deadline.
Widespread experimentation supports the forecast but does not alone establish a large change in educational practice. Improved test scores are not required.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence establishes substantial, widespread changes attributable to AI in teaching, learning practices, or assessment.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence covering the contextual deadline shows that AI remains peripheral and has produced little substantial change in teaching, learning, or assessment.

evidence.locator: Key findings, Assessment has changed substantially
evidence.explanation: This is strong evidence of perceived assessment changes among surveyed UK undergraduates. The survey was conducted before the post, so its later publication does not make it evidence of subsequent forecast fulfillment.

evidence.locator: AI Frees Up Time for What Matters Most to Educators
evidence.explanation: The survey reports AI use by 59% of US K–12 educators during the 2025–2026 school year and perceived time savings among most users. This supports meaningful effects on educators' work, but does not establish their magnitude or changes in classroom practice.

The February–March teacher survey indicates that formal institutional responses remain limited. This constrains claims of comprehensive institutional transformation, although informal disruption could itself constitute a large impact.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Post-publication evidence documenting substantial, widespread changes in ordinary teaching, learning, or assessment could establish early fulfillment. Otherwise, assess the accumulated evidence at the contextual deadline of February 2, 2031.
